content.title: Heat dome out west is headed for Texas. Here's what to expect.
content.text: San Antonio temperatures will be solidly in the 80s by 5 p.m. Thursday, according to the National Blend of Models, a composite weather forecast model.National Blend of Models/Pivotal WeatherA heat dome caused by a strong system of high atmospheric pressure will make its way to Texas in the coming days, leading to near-record heat. Meanwhile, a lack of rain in the forecast and relatively low humidity levels this week means we’ll also have a persistent threat of fast-spreading wildfires.Watch MoreSan Antonio on Thursday should have sunny skies accompanied by easy southwest winds of 5 mph. Daytime temperatures will continue trending unseasonably warmer, peaking Thursday near 83 degrees, which is almost 10 degrees hotter than normal. Overnight temperatures will be closer to normal, with predawn temps bottoming out at 55 degrees.Article continues below this adGet Digital Access and Stay Informed With Trusted Local News.Get Digital Access and Stay Informed With Trusted Local News.ONLY 25¢Heat dome on the moveA ridge of high pressure in the middle levels of the atmosphere, which produced extreme heat in Southern California earlier this week will crawl across Arizona on Thursday, bringing the heat dome to the desert Southwest.A heat dome occurs in a system of high atmospheric pressure. The pressure causes air to sink toward the ground, where the compression of air causes temperatures to increase. A resulting “dome” of high pressure ends up trapping the water vapor in the warm air like a pot lid, and denying any chances for rain clouds to form in the upper atmosphere.Article continues below this ad“The strengthening lower-level thermal ridge and mixing with the warming mid-levels lead to a warming trend with above-average temperatures returning,” the National Weather Service said in a forecast bulletin Wednesday. “Local fire weather issues continue in the short term into the long term.”Despite the increase in southerly winds, humidity levels will remain low Thursday, forecasters said. The Texas A&M Forest Service has placed most of the state under a moderate risk of fast-spreading wildfires.Article continues below this ad"While winds are generally light, keeping fire weather conditions elevated in most areas through Sunday, they increase along the Rio Grande on Sunday to possibly yield near critical fire weather conditions there," the weather service said. "Increasing moisture should return higher minimum humidities next week."Friday and beyondFriday in San Antonio should be sunny, with balmy southwest winds of 5 mph helping to push daytime temperatures to as high as 89 degrees. Should that forecast hold up, that afternoon high would be almost 15 degrees warmer than normal for March 20 — and only 4 degrees shy of the daily heat record set 50 years ago.Article continues below this adOvernight temperatures again would be closer to normal, bottoming out at 57 before dawn Saturday, forecasters said.The mid-level ridge of high pressure will expand over Texas on Friday and through the weekend, the weather service said. Saturday and Sunday will both feature near-record temperatures in South Texas.In this weather satellite photo taken just after noon Wednesday, a system of high atmospheric pressure has cleared the skies over much of the southwest corner of the United States. The system could keep skies over Texas clear throughout the weekend.Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites/CIRA and NOAASan Antonio could see peak daytime temperatures on both weekend days as high as 92 degrees, which would put them within only a few degrees of matching the daily records for March 21-22. Gusty south-southeast winds of around 5 to 10 mph are expected to return and should deliver more moisture-rich air from the Gulf Coast.Article continues below this ad"The mid-level ridge flattens as moist southerly lower-level flow increases to result in daytime temperatures backing off from the record levels, though they remain well above average early to middle of next week," the weather service said, adding that forecast models continue to keep rain chances out of next week's outlook.March 19, 2026Texas Weather Science EditorRoberto Villalpando is the Texas weather science editor for the Houston Chronicle, San Antonio Express-News and Austin American-Statesman. He supervises a team of three newsroom meteorologists and can be reached at roberto.villalpando@houstonchronicle.com. Working out of Austin, the Northwestern University alum joined the Chronicle in 2023 and has more than 25 years of experience covering Texas news and weather as a breaking news editor, multimedia producer, graphic artist, copy editor and reporter.
